package_info.package_name: N/A (GitHub repository manipulation, not a specific package)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire repository is considered malicious due to the intentional manipulation of commit metadata (timestamps and author identity) to create a false sense of trust and credibility, potentially luring developers into using code from untrustworthy or attacker-controlled sources.

execution_context.file_location: local git environment (before pushing to GitHub)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
set git GIT_AUTHOR_DATE=2010-04-19 17:18:43
set git GIT_COMMITTER_DATE=2010-04-19 17:18:43
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At commit-time, the code sets environment variables to falsify the commit timestamp, resulting in GitHub displaying fake historical activity for the user.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior is suspicious because it manipulates the historical record of code contributions, making it appear as if the user has been active for much longer than reality.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal commits should reflect the actual time of contribution; falsifying timestamps undermines trust in repository history.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, developers may backdate commits for migration or archival purposes, but this is not standard practice.
key_indicators: Unusual or impossible commit dates (e.g., before account/repo creation)

execution_context.file_location: local git environment (before pushing to GitHub)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
git config user.name <spoofed_username>
git config user.email <spoofed_email>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At commit-time, the code sets the git user.name and user.email to impersonate another GitHub user, causing the commit to appear as if authored by a trusted third party.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Impersonating another user in commit metadata is a clear attempt to mislead others about the origin and trustworthiness of code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal commits should accurately reflect the true author; spoofing identity is deceptive and undermines code provenance.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, a developer may use a shared account or generic email for organizational commits, but impersonating specific users is not legitimate.
key_indicators: Commits attributed to well-known users who are not actual contributors
Mismatch between commit signature and displayed author

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Commits should reflect accurate authorship and timing; this process intentionally subverts that expectation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Standard commit usage is legitimate, but when combined with spoofed metadata, it becomes malicious.
key_indicators: Commits with mismatched or unverifiable metadata
Commits lacking cryptographic signatures from the displayed author

behavioral_signatures: Commits with timestamps predating account or repository creation
Commits attributed to well-known users who are not actual contributors
Repositories with sudden, high-volume historical activity
file_indicators: Bulk commits with identical or patterned commit messages
Commits lacking cryptographic signatures from the displayed author
network_indicators: N/A (no direct network activity, but may correlate with scraping of public commit data)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for commits with timestamps that are inconsistent with repository or user creation dates. Flag repositories with contributors who have not signed their commits or whose commit signatures do not match the displayed author. Look for sudden spikes in historical activity or contributions from high-profile users who are not otherwise associated with the project. Encourage the use of signed commits and vigilant mode to highlight unverified or spoofed contributions.
